description:
CCPM Team 6 is dedicated to tackling NASA’s challenge of advancing fire safety by exploring how combustion behaves in microgravity and applying these discoveries to improve fire safety in space and on Earth.

Through SIMPLYFIRE, our AI-powered dashboard, we aim to organize, analyze, and interpret NASA’s combustion research, turning complex scientific data into accessible insights.

We believe understanding fire beyond Earth can help create a safer future everywhere.
summary:
SimplyFire is an interactive web dashboard that makes NASA’s space combustion research easy to explore. We built a single browser-based app with five parts: a plain-language guide to combustion and gravity, an interactive lab with a fire-spread simulator, a research explorer that ranks NASA experiments (BASS, Saffire, SAME, FLEX, LUCI and more) against a safety question and scenario, a section on the science and real incidents, and a set of practical conclusions.

It addresses the challenge by turning data from NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics repository and mission pages into something people can use without a science background. Each experiment links back to NASA sources, and missing data is flagged instead of guessed.

This matters because fire is one of the most serious dangers on a spacecraft, and flames behave very differently in microgravity and in the oxygen-rich atmospheres planned for the Moon and Mars. Making this knowledge clear helps students, educators and the public understand how crews will be kept safe.
details:
What it does and how it works
SimplyFire is a web dashboard that teaches how fire behaves in space and what NASA has learned about keeping crews safe. It has five tabs:

-Combustion basics: a plain-language introduction to flames, gravity and fire.

-Interactive lab: sliders and presets for oxygen, pressure and conditions, plus a grid-based module fire simulator. You can place fuel and vents and see how a fire spreads over time. It shows an average of 20 runs and whether an alarm was raised.

-Research explorer: you pick a fire-safety question and the dashboard ranks NASA investigations (BASS, BASS-II, Saffire, SAME, FLEX, CFI-G, SPICE, LUCI and others) by how well they match your question and scenario.

-Information & foundations: the science, links to NASA experiment pages, real incidents and Earth applications of this research.

-Conclusions: practical fire precautions for human space exploration.

--Benefits and intended impact
It turns scattered NASA combustion research into something students, educators and curious people can explore without a science background. It also shows why fire safety matters for Moon and Mars missions, and where the evidence is still thin. We want people to leave understanding that fire in space is not just “fire on Earth with no gravity.”

--Tools and technology
The whole project is one self-contained HTML file written in HTML, CSS and JavaScript. It uses the canvas element for the starfield, the fire grid and the trend graph. It needs no server, no database and no external libraries, so it runs in any modern browser and works offline. The experiment data was compiled by hand from NASA sources, including the Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository and NASA mission pages. [Add any hardware, design tools or AI assistants your team used.]

--How it is creative

It combines education, simulation and research exploration in one interface instead of a static report.

The research explorer ranks experiments with transparent, rule-based scoring (question match, evidence quality, safety relevance), not a black box.

It treats partial gravity (LUCI) as its own category, and it marks data gaps instead of guessing.

--Factors we considered

-Accuracy and honesty: missing data is flagged, and the simulator is labeled an educational model, not a risk prediction.

-Sources: every experiment links back to NASA material.

-Accessibility: the page is written in plain language and the interactive parts have screen-reader labels.

-Limits: airflow velocity is not recorded as numbers in the dataset, so it is not scored.

-Applications on Earth: it shows what this research has led to, such as water mist extinguishers and smoke detection.
